candidates.quote: When a man takes an oath, Meg, he’s holding his own self in his own hands.
candidates.author: Robert Bolt
candidates.locator: Act Two, to his daughter Meg (Heinemann, 1960)
candidates.speaker: Sir Thomas More
candidates.whyThisMonth: It gives a reader a physical picture of what is actually at stake when they are being pressed to say a thing they do not believe.

candidates.quote: In every town, every village, every mud hut in the world there is always a man who loves children and who will fight to make a good world for them.
candidates.author: Lillian Hellman
candidates.locator: Act Three, his farewell to his children (Random House, 1941)
candidates.speaker: Kurt Müller
candidates.whyThisMonth: A father leaving for danger tells his children the thing that makes the danger bearable: he is not the only one, and never has been.

candidates.quote: Oh, I’ve never forgotten for long at a time that living is struggle.
candidates.author: Thornton Wilder
candidates.locator: Act III, near the end (Harper and Brothers, 1942)
candidates.speaker: Mr Antrobus
candidates.whyThisMonth: It says the difficulty was never a mistake in the plan, and a reader who expected ease can set that expectation down and get on with the day.

candidates.quote: Zeus, who guided men to think, / who has laid it down that wisdom / comes alone through suffering.
candidates.author: Aeschylus
candidates.locator: lines 176 to 178, the Hymn to Zeus, in the Oresteia (University of Chicago Press, 1953)
candidates.speaker: the Chorus
candidates.whyThisMonth: At six in the morning of a hard stretch it offers the oldest consolation in the theatre: the difficulty is not wasted, it is the road to the understanding.

candidates.quote: The fairest action of our human life / Is scorning to revenge an injury; / For who forgives without a further strife, / His adversary’s heart to him doth tie.
candidates.author: Elizabeth Cary
candidates.work: The Tragedy of Mariam, the Fair Queen of Jewry
candidates.locator: the Chorus that closes Act IV, lines 1 to 4 (1613 quarto)
candidates.speaker: Chorus
candidates.whyThisMonth: It names the bravest thing a wronged person can do before breakfast, which is to decline the repayment that is owed to them.

candidates.quote: What sap / went through that little thread / to make the cherry red!
candidates.author: Marianne Moore
candidates.whyThisMonth: It points at the thinnest possible thread and asks what came through it, which is a fair question to ask about a person still standing.

candidates.quote: To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.
candidates.author: Alfred Tennyson
candidates.speaker: Ulysses
candidates.whyThisMonth: Four verbs and a refusal: it is the plainest thing in English to say to yourself on the morning of something you would rather not begin.

candidates.quote: We never know how high we are / Till we are called to rise; / And then, if we are true to plan, / Our statures touch the skies.
candidates.author: Emily Dickinson
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 4, Poems by Emily Dickinson, Third Series, ed. Mabel Loomis Todd (Roberts Brothers, 1896)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The reader who doubts they are equal to the day is told the measurement only happens once the day asks, and not before.

candidates.quote: Just like moons and like suns, / With the certainty of tides, / Just like hopes springing high, / Still I’ll rise.
candidates.author: Maya Angelou
candidates.locator: lines 9 to 12, And Still I Rise (Random House, 1978)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It puts getting up again in the same class as the tide and the sunrise, which is exactly the register a person needs at six in the morning.

candidates.quote: We know what trembles on the scales, / and what we must steel ourselves to face. / The bravest hour strikes on our clocks: / may courage not abandon us!
candidates.author: Anna Akhmatova
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 4, Poems of Akhmatova (Little, Brown, 1973)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A poem literally titled Courage that asks for it rather than claims it, which is the honest posture for anyone about to walk into a hard day.

candidates.quote: Although the wind / blows terribly here, / the moonlight also leaks / between the roof planks / of this ruined house.
candidates.author: Izumi Shikibu
candidates.locator: the complete tanka, The Ink Dark Moon (Vintage Classics, 1990)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The same gaps that let the weather in are the gaps that let the light in, which is the most useful thing to know about a life that is not holding up well.

candidates.quote: A joy it will be one day, perhaps, to remember even this.
candidates.author: Virgil
candidates.locator: Book 1, line 203 of the Latin, to his men after the storm (Viking, 2006)
candidates.speaker: Aeneas
candidates.whyThisMonth: A leader with no good news lends his men the future instead, and the word perhaps keeps the promise honest enough to lean on.

candidates.quote: The world stands out on either side / No wider than the heart is wide; / Above the world is stretched the sky,— / No higher than the soul is high.
candidates.author: Edna St. Vincent Millay
candidates.locator: the closing verse paragraph, Renascence and Other Poems (Mitchell Kennerley, 1917)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It tells a reader the size of their day is set by the size of their heart, which is the one measurement they can still do something about.

candidates.quote: For I’se still goin’, honey, / I’se still climbin’, / And life for me ain’t been no crystal stair.
candidates.author: Langston Hughes
candidates.locator: the closing three lines, The Crisis, December 1922
candidates.speaker: the mother
candidates.whyThisMonth: The proof offered is not advice but a person still on the stairs, which is the only argument that works on someone who wants to sit down.

candidates.quote: But where danger threatens / That which saves from it also grows.
candidates.author: Friedrich Hölderlin
candidates.locator: lines 3 to 4, Friedrich Hölderlin: Poems and Fragments (Michigan, 1966)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It sends a reader looking for the remedy in the same place as the trouble, and it is the honest Hamburger wording rather than the slogan that circulates.

candidates.quote: Manfully, fearlessly, / The day of trial bear, / For gloriously, victoriously, / Can courage quell despair!
candidates.author: Charlotte Brontë
candidates.locator: the closing four lines, Poems by Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell (Aylott and Jones, 1846)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month’s theme said out loud: it names the day of trial and then names what carries a person through it, with no hedging at all.
